title: Walking into an established way
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Have you been in a company when new owners arrived? What did your team do?

I said: that is a much more hostile situation, going into a company that is already established. This is how we do things around here, don't tell us what to do. There will be immense resistance to change.
A student asked: is that why, when a company changes owners, almost the whole company leaves, and a brand-new team is hired?

A student in telecom said: I have been through this many times. In the start-up mentality you have a dozen or twenty-five people committed, with meaningful stock options. You have a very different level of motivation when you get to thousands of employees. The people who were there from the beginning may have lost that spark.

The student said: it was also very tribal. As soon as a vice president from one company came to another, you knew they were bringing their people and looking to clean things out. You either got in with them in a good way, or started polishing your resume.
I said that in the telecom sector, he saw people go into boardrooms with a machine gun, as a manner of speaking: everybody is gone out of here.
What would you do in your first week if you arrived as the new owner?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write what a new owner would find in your company.
Write what the people who were there at the start have lost, if anything.
Write what you would do on the first day to reduce fear.

check.q: What did I say you face in an established company?
What did a student say is different with thousands of employees?
choices: A different level of motivation than in a start-up

check.q: What did the student say about a new vice president?

recap: Expect resistance when you arrive. Know what start-up spark has been lost.
